title: Why inference matters to platform teams
body:
Purpose
This one-pager reframes the Redwood value proposition specifically for internal platform teams (Platform, SRE, Infra Platform, Internal Developer Platforms). It explains why inference is now a first-class platform concern, the practical costs of ignoring it, and the messaging that helps Platform owners champion Redwood to application teams and execs.

Core insight / thesis
Platform teams face a new axis of operational risk and cost: real-time model serving. Unlike batch ML, inference touches latency SLOs, cost variability, data governance, and developer experience simultaneously. Platform teams that standardize inference as a platform capability win: faster product launches, predictable budgets, and unified observability across AI features. Redwood’s mission is to make that capability simple, reliable, and measurable.

Why Platform teams care (short bullets)
- Latency is a product metric: When search, chat, or assistant features are added, tail latency becomes a user-facing reliability issue.
- Cost leakage is hidden: Uninstrumented inference can blow out cloud GPU spend and per-token charges across many teams.
- Operational complexity scales: Multiple app teams run different models, versions, and configs—creating toil and fragmentation.
- Governance & compliance: Private deployments, key management, and audit trails are mandatory for regulated apps.
- Developer velocity: Teams want self-serve model routes and predictable rollout controls, not bespoke infra for each feature.

Why Redwood (concise positioning statements)
- Unified runtime for teams: One API and one set of tools that works across hosted, reserved, and VPC/private installs so Platform squads can expose a single capability to developers.
- Economics-first engineering: Controls (batching, caching, quantization profiles) and visibility that let Platform own predictable unit costs without sacrificing latency targets.
- Built for operations: Tracing, token-level cost breakdowns, SLO dashboards, and rollout primitives that align with Platform runbooks.
- Safe defaults + guardrails: Policies, RBAC, and private control planes reduce blast radius from feature experiments.

Messages to surface by audience
- Platform Lead (executive): "Reduce unpredictable AI spend and centralize SLA accountability while enabling teams to ship AI features faster."
- SRE/Infra Engineer: "Drop-in runtime with tooling for tracing, fallbacks, and capacity planning—fewer firefights during peak traffic."
- Developer/Product Teams: "Self-serve endpoints with versioning and canary rollouts—ship experiments without bespoke infra."

Sales battlecard snippets (quick rebuttals)
- Objection: "We can run models on our existing GPU pool."
  Rebuttal: "Yes, but without unified batching, KV cache, and model-aware kernel selection you leave 30–60% of throughput on the table and multiply operational variance. Redwood captures that efficiency and makes it repeatable across teams."
- Objection: "We are worried about vendor lock-in and data residency."
  Rebuttal: "Redwood Private runs in your VPC or on-prem, with customer-managed KMS and audit logs; the API and rollout model remain the same if you migrate between modes."

Differentiators to emphasize (practical phrasing)
- Same API everywhere: Developers don’t need to learn separate flows for hosted vs. private.
- Unit economics visibility: Per-route/token cost breakdowns that feed internal chargeback and show ROI of quantization or caching.
- Reliability primitives: Canary rollouts, A/B traffic splits, automatic model fallbacks to keep critical paths alive.

Proof points & adoption milestones (internal metrics to track)
- Time-to-first-inference: Reduce from X weeks to Y days for new AI features.
- Cost variance reduction: % reduction in monthly inference spend volatility after centralizing on Redwood.
- Mean-time-to-recovery for model-serving incidents: target 50% reduction after rollout of Redwood SLO dashboards and playbooks.

Quick integration pattern for Platform engineers
1) Deploy Redwood Private control plane in VPC with KMS integration.
2) Configure per-team model routes and resource pools; set default batching/cache profiles.
3) Expose a simple internal endpoint catalog and SDK to developer teams.
4) Enable tracing and cost tagging by product route for chargeback.
5) Run a one-week pilot with two product teams and an SLO incident drill.

Suggested tactical collateral to build
- "Platform playbook: Rolling out Redwood across an engineering org" (checklist + runbook).
- Sample Terraform module for Private install and KMS.
- One-page internal pitch deck for Eng+Product leadership.
- Postmortem template that includes model-route cost and cache hit metrics.

Open questions / follow-ups
- Pick three customer examples (internal or external) where consolidating inference reduced cost variance—collect anonymized numbers.
- Map common compliance requirements across top accounts to Redwood Private controls.
- Draft an SLO template (latency, error-rate, cost-per-1000-tokens) for Platform teams to adopt.

Recommended next steps
- Run a 4-week internal pilot with Platform + two product teams to validate integration pattern.
- Create engineering-ready collateral (Terraform module, SDK guide) and an executive one-pager for the pilot sponsor.
- Track the three adoption metrics above and prepare a short case study for GTM playbook.
